video.title: Variables and input: Programs that remember and ask
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Salma Haddad — the students’ maths teacher (main character)
Mr Okafor — the students’ science teacher (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice, talking to the student (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.narration: A game greets you by name, and knows your score. How does it remember? It keeps each thing in a variable, a name with a value inside.
Today: variables, and programs that ask you questions.
A variable is a name that holds a value. The equals sign puts the value on the right into the name on the left. After that, wherever you write the name, Python uses its value.
A variable can change. Score equals score plus ten takes the old score, adds ten, and stores the new score. The old value is gone: a variable holds one value at a time.
To ask the person using your program a question, use input. The program waits until they type an answer and press Enter. Store the answer in a variable, and use it.

Here’s the trap. input always gives back text, even if you type a number. Text plus text sticks together: five plus three in quotes gives fifty-three! Turn the answer into a number with int, and the sum works.
Quick check! Score is twenty. Then score equals score plus five. What does print score show?
Twenty-five. In Python, the equals sign doesn’t mean the same as in maths. It means: work out the right side, then store it in the name on the left.
Now your programs can talk back. Ask for a name and say hello. Ask for an age and say how old they’ll be in ten years. Ask for phone credit and a price, and say if there’s enough.
Choose clear names: score, age, price. Names can’t have spaces, so use an underscore, like phone underscore credit. Capital letters count: Score and score are two different names.
In the app, open Bug hunt and try bugs five and six. In one, a name is spelt wrong. In the other, text and a number are added together. Read the error, fix it and run it again.
Your turn. A program asks your age with input, then prints age plus one. You type thirteen. What happens?

scenes.on_screen_text: A name · = stores · input gives text · int
scenes.narration: An error. Remember: a variable is a name with one value at a time. The equals sign stores. input asks a question and always gives text. Use int to turn it into a number.
Try it yourself: write a program that asks for your name and your age, then says how old you’ll be in ten years. Try it on a friend or someone at home!

checkpoints.prompt: score = 20, then score = score + 5. What does print(score) show?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — it takes the old value, 20, adds 5 and stores 25.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — = stores: the old 20 plus 5 becomes the new score, 25.

checkpoints.prompt: age = input("Age? "), then print(age + 1). You type 13. What happens?

options.text: An error: text plus a number

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — age is the text "13", and text + a number is a TypeError. Use int() first.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — input gave text, so age + 1 stops with a TypeError. int(age) fixes it.
